articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of Iran General License FF-1. This new general license authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.
This action follows a series of recent adjustments to Iran-related sanctions, including designations and the issuance of other general licenses earlier in October.

The issuance of wind-down licenses typically provides a limited timeframe for U.S. persons to conclude transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions regulations, emphasizing the need for swift compliance.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for North Korea IT Worker Fraud and DRC Destabilization
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in North Korea's illicit IT worker schemes and those supporting destabilizing activities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The North Korea-related designations include individuals leading Russia-based delegations of DPRK IT workers, facilitating financial transfers and sanctions evasion.

Additionally, OFAC designated the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Rwanda and Zigama Credit and Savings Society for their support of the M23 rebel group, which is contributing to the conflict in the Eastern DRC.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA). MMZA was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company, JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, rendering MMZA a blocked person by operation of law, even though it was not directly listed on the SDN List at the time of the transactions.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, highlighting the importance of thorough sanctions diligence, especially in acquisitions and oversight of foreign affiliates.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Obligations
body: OFAC has amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) as part of its ongoing review of published guidance.
The revisions clarify the distinction between blocking and rejecting transactions, the treatment of blocked funds, and reporting requirements for U.S. financial institutions.

Key updates include guidance on maintaining segregated, interest-bearing accounts for blocked funds, the types of supporting documentation required for reports, and the distinction between a customer inquiry and an actual payment instruction.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations.
The action also included the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.
These comprehensive updates reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, balancing enforcement with humanitarian considerations and evolving geopolitical landscapes.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: OFAC announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and issued associated General Licenses.

The designations target entities such as BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP and SHANGHAI ZHISUAN TECHNOLOGY CO LTD, with blocking of property and restrictions on loans and foreign exchange transactions.

General License 1 authorizes certain transactions pursuant to Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, while General License 2 authorizes the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: OFAC issued Venezuela-related General License 60A, authorizing transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.
Additionally, OFAC issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, providing further clarification on Venezuela sanctions.
This amendment underscores a humanitarian carve-out within the broader Venezuela sanctions regime, allowing for critical aid in times of natural disaster.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.
The State Department designated Cuba's BANCO INTERNACIONAL DE COMERCIO S.A. (BICSA) for providing services to Iran's Karafarin Bank.
These actions reflect ongoing efforts to counter illicit financial networks and address activities deemed contrary to U.S. foreign policy interests in both Iran and Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly President from Sanctions List
body: OFAC announced the removal of Jorge Jesus Rodriguez Gomez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.
This delisting is seen as a significant step in U.S. engagement with Venezuela, following earlier removals of sanctions on other Venezuelan officials and entities.
The move signals a potential shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela, moving from punitive economic containment to more structured engagement.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: OFAC announced new designations under its Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism sanctions programs.
The designations target individuals and entities supporting Cartel del Noreste through various businesses, including horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector in Mexico.
These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based company, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.
The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was a blocked person by virtue of its majority ownership by a designated entity.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to a coordinated resolution with the Department of Justice.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 for Sanctions Violations

These violations involved transactions related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
The settlement underscores the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs for financial institutions operating globally.

This settlement highlights the necessity for companies to accurately report blocked property and fully cooperate with OFAC investigations.

The package adds 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, including 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
